title: Ancient Trees in the Netherlands: Cities to Explore
meta_description: The Netherlands is the wrong country for ancient trees and has them anyway. Sheltered survivors across 14 mapped cities, oldest of all a 1638 pear tree.
intro: The Netherlands is the wrong country for ancient trees and has them anyway. Half of it was seabed, peat bog or open water within the last thousand years, the soil is young, the water table sits close under the roots, and North Sea storms arrive with nothing in the way to slow them down. What survived did so under shelter, and that shapes the entire list: a pear tree inside an almshouse courtyard, a cycad potted in a botanical garden in 1704 and never repotted since, lindens pollarded for three centuries because a village square needed its shade. Dutch ancient trees are tended survivors rather than forest giants, which is why so many stand behind a gate you have to find rather than out in open parkland. It also explains the oldest one on this list: a fruit tree.
